projects.name: Barbados Coastal Fisheries Project
projects.description: The passage of Hurricane Beryl on 1 July 2024 resulted in significant losses and damages to Barbados’ coastal assets and infrastructure. Some of the most significant impacts were felt by the Oistins Fisheries complex south of Bridgetown and the Barbados Fisheries Complex in Bridgetown where most damages were concentrated. The Barbados Fisheries Complex comprises the primary harbour facility for the fishing fleet, fish landing facilities, and a market. It is estimated that more than 200 vessels owned by local fishers suffered damage. These impacts reveal significant vulnerabilities, particularly related to a lack of a natural sheltered harbour and safe harbour facilities. To comprehensively address the full scope of the challenge outlined above is beyond the scope of this project and would likely require broader and more sustained support. However, this project aims to provide tangible and catalytic early recovery by focusing on strategic reinstatement and resilience upgrades of select physical infrastructures and assets including equipment to facilitate business continuity and resilient operations, complemented and enabled by targeted capacity building, and strategic partnerships.  The project’s design is guided by the principle that early recovery interventions that enable ‘building back better’ by incorporating increased resilience and enhancing disaster preparedness will both alleviate present impacts from Hurricane Beryl as well as reduce the risk of the adverse effects of future natural disasters on the local fishing community in Barbados.  USD $2.93 Million will be deployed in a targeted manner over the course of one year to contribute to resilient reconstruction focused on materials, equipment and installations that can be readily procured and installed and will be complementary and/or catalytic with broader reconstruction and resilience building efforts. It is expected that the project will directly impact 100 boat owners, 300 fishers, more than 150 fish vendor/processors and will improve the skills of 100 industry stakeholders including the Barbados National Union of Fisherfolk Organization (BARNUFO). The entire fishing industry with a participation of 6000  persons stands to benefit from the improvement in disaster preparedness protocols and safer and more resilient facilities. The project will also have a positive indirect benefit to restaurants, domestic consumers (close to 100,000 households) and the vital tourism sector. The tourism sector comprises close to 156 properties of which 64 are hotels; stay over arrivals of 636,606 and cruise arrivals 441,677 people recorded in 2024 .  The proposal will form part of a wider Government of Barbados Fisheries Recovery Plan for the repair and replacement of vessels, rehabilitation of the marine based components of the Bridgetown Fisheries Complex (breakwater, finger pier, and slip way); rehabilitation of landing facilities and coastal protection along with capacity building in disaster management, and is complementary to initiatives funded by other international partners such as the World Bank.

projects.name: Global Biodiversity Framework Early Action Support (GBF-EAS)
projects.description:
The recent “Little Book on Investing in Nature” estimates the global annual biodiversity financing gap at US$700 billion. The CBD Panel of Experts on Resource Mobilization highlighted that 
implementation of the new biodiversity targets under the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) will require additional financial resources, increased resource efficiency, and a reduction of biodiversity-harmful financial flows. Reducing the biodiversity finance gap can only be achieved through transformative change across 
economies and society.
To develop a clear picture of how to achieve the targets of the CBD’s GBF, a detailed assessment of the policy and institutional national context, a biodiversity expenditures review and financial needs are required as well as development and implementation of finance plans. CBD Parties face the following key barriers to sustainable financing of nature-positive policies and practices: (a) limited awareness, coordination, and capacity among national stakeholders to address gaps in biodiversity financing; (b) insufficient knowledge and systematic (c) lack of systematic measurement and reporting 
of the negative impacts of finance contributing to biodiversity loss; (d) biodiversity finance needs are imprecisely defined and poorly understood; (e) limited knowledge, use and mainstreaming of country-specific biodiversity finance solutions; and (f) limited exchange and uptake of global best practices in the sustainable 
financing of biodiversity.

Given the need for a comprehensive and multi-stakeholder strategic approach to resource mobilization, Target 19 requests all countries to develop national biodiversity finance plans (BFPs). These BFPs should assess the root causes of biodiversity loss, identify national biodiversity finance gaps, and articulate strategies on how to reduce the gaps through a suite of finance solutions aimed at reducing flow of resources that cause harm to biodiversity; generating additional resources; and enhancing the effectiveness and efficiency of resource use. To respond to this need and based on the experience of UNDP’s Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN) and other relevant methodologies, this project aims to support a global programme that will establish a transformative 
process for biodiversity finance in all participating eligible countries, involving all relevant stakeholders such as Ministries of Finance and Environment, and the private and financial sectors through a socially and gender-inclusive approach. The project will support countries in baseline diagnostics, capacity and institutional strengthening, and developing finance plans to mobilize resources at scale to implement the GBF.

projects.name: TTO Ethical Recruitment and Work Permit Support in Aruba
projects.description:
Work Permit Support:
1. IOM Aruba will provide additional capacity and technical support to the Government of Aruba to undocumented migrants with work permit procedures, including for their family members, as allowed in the new policy. Additionally, beneficiaries requiring CBI assistance in order to access permits will receive a small grant. The level of subsidy for the permits will depend on the beneficiaries' vulnerability, assessed using predefined criteria. Importantly, the financial responsibility for these permits will not rest solely on IOM; private sector partners will also contribute to the costs.  
2. IOM Aruba will provide targeted support to the Government of Aruba for the implementation of the new work permit policy, enhancing the government's capacity through technical inputs and assistance. This support aims to streamline processes, improve policy implementation, and ensure that the work permit system effectively addresses the needs of both migrants and the host community. The assistance will include in-kind technical support, such as providing resources, tools, and specialized expertise to facilitate the policy rollout. Additionally, IOM Aruba will offer technical assistance, including capacity-building activities, training sessions, and advisory services to government officials. This collaborative effort is designed to strengthen the government's capacity to manage work permits efficiently, foster economic inclusion, and promote a more organized and responsive labor market in Aruba.

Ethical Recruitment Programme:
The IOM Ethical Recruitment Program aims to promote fair and responsible hiring practices by working closely with employers and recruiters to ensure that labor migration is safe, transparent, and equitable. The program focuses on preventing exploitation and abuse of workers by promoting principles such as no recruitment fees for job seekers, clear employment terms, and respect for workers’ rights. Through training, capacity building, and guidelines, the program helps private sector partners adhere to ethical standards that protect both migrants and employers, fostering a fair and sustainable labor market that benefits all parties involved.

projects.name: REG Caribbean BluEFin - Caribbean Blue Economy Financing Project
projects.description:
The GEF-7 (#10782) Project also known as the "Caribbean Blue Economy Financing Project” is implemented in The Bahamas (Dominican Republic), Grenada, St. Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines. The objective is to create and strengthen nature-based Blue Economy opportunities and approaches in the Caribbean through innovative financing mechanisms, and targets The Bahamas,  Dominican Republic,  Grenada,  St. Lucia,  St. Vincent and Grenadines. As the concepts of “Blue Economy” and “Blue Businesses” are in early stages of development in the insular Caribbean region, the BluEFin Project aims to facilitate coordination of activities directed at identifying sources of economic value in the marine and coastal areas and facilitate development of long-term solutions and sustainable financing mechanisms. The coordination will efficiently consider the best use of Blue Economy opportunities for conservation financing mechanisms, marrying 2 core international commitments. The Project also supports Caribbean countries by building on and delivering the GEF Caribbean Large Marine Ecosystem (CLME+), Strategic Action Programmmes' (SAP) project implementation targets. The Project brings together public and private sector partners of the Caribbean Sustainable Finance Architecture (CSFA) to identify feasible Caribbean-based regional and national Financing Mechanisms (FMs).  Component #3 develops a Blue Economy Hub; while Component 4 supports a Community of learning, and strengthening of regional networks on the value of Blue Economy in Caribbean regional financing and development. Support will also be provided for high level discussions among Caribbean Leaders on the Caribbean's 30x30 Vision for Ocean Governance (as a follow on to the Caribbean Challenge Initiative with its 2020 target) and CBF will promote regional FMs as a vehicle and targeting NGOs and the private sector. The implementation partner is the Caribbean Biodiversity Fund.

Component 1 of the Project applies Blue Economy principles to develop at least three regional Ocean finance mechanisms that generate long‑term, reliable funding for marine and coastal biodiversity, including transboundary resources, creates enabling systems, incentives, and policies to facilitate private sector participation in Blue Economy business opportunities (Component 2), and establishes a regional Caribbean Blue Economy Hub to showcase, support, and regularly update information on blue business opportunities and investments that enhance conservation and sustainable use of marine and coastal ecosystems (Component 3). In addition, the project promotes socialising, scaling, and replication of the BluEFin approach through a regional community of learning on conservation finance (Component 4), and ensures efficient, gender‑responsive monitoring, reporting, and independent evaluation to support timely, adaptive implementation across all components (Component 5).

To strengthen the capacities of selected countries in the Caribbean and the Arab region to leverage trade policy measures and harness transport and logistic to be better prepared for and respond to supply chain disruptions and build sustainable and resilient food supply chains.

projects.name: Antigua and Barbuda Sustainable Low-Emission Island Mobility Project
projects.description: The Project, "Supporting Antigua and Barbuda's Sustainable Low-Emission Island Mobility and transition" (GEF-7 #10281) addresses priorities to transition Antigua and Barbuda's transportation and energy sectors towards a low-carbon trajectory. Total allocation is $3,245,000. As a small island developing state (SIDS), Antigua and Barbuda’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions represent just 0.0015% of the world’s total. However, the country’s per capita GHG emissions are higher than those of Spain and France. Antigua and Barbuda’s biggest challenge is the energy sector, which, due to fossil fuel combustion activities, accounts for 76% of the country’s total emissions. These two sectors rely almost entirely on imported petroleum-based fuels. Electricity generation is responsible for close to 40% of total GHG emissions generated from heavy fuel oil thermal power plants and experiences high distribution grid inefficiencies. As a result, the emission intensity per MWh of the electricity consumed is around 1000 kg of CO2 per MWh generated, almost double the global average. The transport sub-sector is similarly problematic, with road transport accounting for more than 20% of total national GHG emissions. Under business as usual (BAU) conditions overall emissions are expected to rise considerably over the next decade, primarily due to increases in electricity demand and growth in individual transport usage. BAU estimations indicate that the private vehicle fleet could grow at an annual rate of 6.5% per year.  Project activities will put in motion the transformation of both the power and transport sectors of Antigua and Barbuda, transitioning these from the current scenario of fossil fuel dependence to a future where low-carbon and climate resilient technologies are predominant. The Project will strengthen and inform political and public support for the uptake of low-carbon and climate-resilient electric transport and power generation systems. Activities include: reducing technological, financial and modal barriers through technical assistance and investment in pilot projects; building local capacity in related areas; and implementing regulations, policies and standards to secure a sustainable transition into the future and avoid potential environmental contamination. The Project has been extended to 30 April 2027

projects.name: REG Advancing a Regional Approach Towards the Green Hydrogen Economy in Latin America and the Caribbean
projects.description:
The Project aims to create an enabling environment to foster the development of a regional green hydrogen economy and to build the capacity of participating countries to attract investment, develop policies, and implement strategic projects. Jamaica and Trinidad & Tobago are among seven countries in the Latin America & Caribbean region (including Bolivia, Chile, El Salvador, Honduras and Uruguay) participating in the regional initiative funded by the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and implemented by UNEP. The use of green hydrogen as an energy vector to support countries' decarbonization pathways is a genuinely new vision that was endorsed by many countries at the UNFCCC COP26 meeting.  Total regional Project budget is US$2,049,971.

As a Group A (early stage) country (including El Salvador & Honduras), the Government of Jamaica is advancing the development of a national green hydrogen economy as part of its broader transition toward a low-carbon, resilient, and diversified energy system. Green hydrogen presents a strategic opportunity to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors, strengthen energy security, and unlock new areas of industrial development and investment. To support this emerging sector in a coordinated and inclusive manner, the establishment of a National Green Hydrogen Inter-Institutional Working Group is proposed, to serve as a national advisory and coordination mechanism, bringing together key public and private stakeholders to support policy coherence, strategic planning, and informed decision-making related to green hydrogen development in the country. The national partners are the Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation (MEGJC), now Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development (MEGID); Ministry of Energy, Transport & Telecommunications (METT) and the Ministry of Water, Environment & Climate Change (MWECC).

As a Group B (more advanced) country (including Chile, Bolivia, Uruguay), Trinidad & Tobago is a regional energy leader with a strong foothold in petrochemicals and strategically positioned to spearhead the development of a green hydrogen economy in the LAC region. Leveraging its existing oil and gas infrastructure, operational expertise, and favorable economic conditions, the nation can potentially transform into a green energy superpower. Trinidad & Tobago's competitive advantage includes: its energy sector contribution of 40% of GDP and 80% of export earnings; its strong heritage in oil and gas production and petrochemical exports (ammonia and methanol); its established infrastructure which offers a competitive edge in the emerging hydrogen market; the strategic positioning of the Point Lisas Industrial Estate, poised to be a regional hub for green hydrogen and downstream products; and its thriving energy ecosystem and existing markets with trade relations and export routes. Trinidad & Tobago's lead in existing infrastructure also provides a head start in the green hydrogen market. The national partner is the Ministry of Planning & Development (MPD), now the Ministry of Planning, Economic Affairs & Development (MPEAD).

projects.name: REG Implementation of the Strategic Action Programme to ensure Integrated and Sustainable Management of the Transboundary Water Resources of the Amazon River Basin Considering Climate Variability and Change
projects.description:
The GEF-6 (#9770) Project is implemented in Guyana and Suriname and other member states of the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO) i.e. Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Venezuela. It is implementing the agreed Strategic Action Plan (SAP) by promoting Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) and source‑to‑sea approaches that improve ecological, social and economic benefits across the basin. The Project applies basin‑wide IWRM principles to develop and strengthen a community‑to‑cabinet innovative water governance model that reinforces institutional and policy frameworks, supports the establishment of water authorities where needed, and introduces incentive‑based financing mechanisms such as water funds, green/climate bonds and payments for ecosystem services to generate long‑term support for SAP implementation (Component 1). It further builds community resilience and enhances protection of bio‑aquatic ecosystems through up‑scaled forecasting and alert systems for floods and droughts, natural infrastructure and adaptation measures in coastal and glacier‑dependent areas, and groundwater source protection solutions that reduce contamination risks in vulnerable urban centers (Component 2). In addition, the project establishes integrated, basin‑wide environmental monitoring and reporting systems for water quality, hydro‑meteorology, erosion and sediment transport, bio‑aquatic ecosystems, and priority headwater and wetland areas, providing compatible indicators and data to inform science‑policy decision‑making and reporting under the SDGs and relevant conventions (Component 3). The project also promotes long‑term sustainability of SAP implementation through a comprehensive indicator‑based monitoring and reporting framework, innovative ICT applications and web portals, and targeted communication and marketing products that facilitate knowledge sharing and stakeholder engagement at regional and national levels (Component 4). The total Project budget is $11,735,780, with Guyana and Suriname benefitting from regional scope activities.

Local implementing partners are the Guyana Ministry of Public Works and Suriname Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Business and International Cooperation (BIBIS)

projects.name: BARBADOS DECENT WORK COUNTRY PROGRAMME, 2025-2030
projects.description:
The Barbados Decent Work Country Programme (DWCP) for 2025–2030 establishes the common commitment of the Government of Barbados, employers’ and workers’ organizations, and the International Labour Organization (ILO) to promote Decent Work. It provides a strategic framework to support inclusive, resilient, and sustainable development, aligned with national priorities and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The DWCP focuses on four key priorities:

Productive employment and sustainable enterprises – Promoting job creation, entrepreneurship, and enterprise development, with emphasis on youth, women, and vulnerable groups.
Social protection – Strengthening the coverage, adequacy, and sustainability of social protection systems, and enhancing resilience to economic and climate-related shocks.
Rights at work and labour standards – Advancing compliance with international labour standards, improving working conditions, and reinforcing labour administration and inspection.
Social dialogue and tripartism – Strengthening collaboration among government, employers, and workers to support effective labour market governance and consensus-based policymaking.

Through these priorities, the DWCP aims to expand decent work opportunities, reduce inequalities, and strengthen institutional capacity in Barbados.

projects.name: REG The Smart Seas Toolkit for Disaster Resilience and Digital Inclusion project
projects.description:
The Smart Seas Toolkit (SST) for Disaster Resilience (“Smart Seas”) project is a joint initiative of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), Caribbean Telecommunications Union (CTU) and the Telecommunications Authority of Trinidad and Tobago (TATT), supported by the Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago which aims to increase the resilience and ultimately preserve the lives of Caribbean small-scale fishers (SSF) through information and communications technologies (ICTs), with emphasis on the enabling environment.

The project will identify gaps which may exist in the maritime communications enabling environment, from which gap-filling recommendations will be produced under consultation with key stakeholders within the region. These recommendations, along with other resources produced during the project, will form part of an online toolkit to strengthen the enabling environment. The project is initially being implemented in Trinidad and Tobago, which serves as the Maritime Rescue Co-ordination Centre (MRCC) for: Barbados, Grenada, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, as well as Trinidad and Tobago. The project outputs and outcomes are expected to be transferable to other Caribbean countries.

Furthermore, the project aims to facilitate the establishment of an international community to tackle the ongoing challenge of inaccessible communications at sea, through technological, service and market innovations. Subsequent phases of the Smart Seas project will introduce a certification program for marine very high frequency (VHF) radio- operation and increase SSF capacity. Later phases will also feature the utilization of cutting-edge communication technologies to close data gaps in the maritime sector that are essential for boosting resilience across the mitigation, preparation, response, and recovery phases of the disaster risk management cycle.

This work will strengthen and enhance national capacities to collect, analyze, access, and use disaster risk knowledge for more inclusive and accessible multi-hazard early warning systems. UNDRR will also continue implementing the roadmap developed by the Centre of Excellence that shifts the focus from responding to disasters only after they occur to making a greater investment in preventative comprehensive disaster and climate risk management. projects.name: 2.7.6 BDS Improved capacity of decision makers to leverage ethical artificial intelligence systems in their national decision-making policies and plans to advance safety, social cohesion and benefits across the society
projects.description:
AI Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM): Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a dynamic technology of the 4th Industrial Revolution. Its effects are forecasted to impact every aspect of society. As the discussions about AI heightens, many SIDS including those in the Caribbean, have yet to develop strategies and national policies to manage the impacts of AI on their society even as the citizens interact with AI in daily life. As an underrepresented stakeholder in the AI ethics debate, Caribbean SIDS must begin to articulate the indigenous knowledge, cultural and ethnic pluralism, and diverse value systems that define the sub-region, in line with global ethical standards.  

AI systems raise new types of ethical issues that include, but are not limited to, their impact on decision-making in employment and labour, social interaction, health care, education, media, freedom of expression, access to information, privacy, democracy, discrimination, and weaponization. Furthermore, new ethical challenges and risks are created by the potential of AI algorithms to reproduce biases, for instance regarding gender, ethnicity, and age, and thus to exacerbate already existing forms of discrimination, identity prejudice and stereotyping. As Caribbean nations expand their adoption of AI tools and other frontier technologies, stakeholders (policymakers, citizens, private sector, academia, and NGOs) must proactively collaborate to create strategies for the humanistic and ethical development and adoption of guidelines, regulations and frameworks.

The Project is implemented by UNEP and aims to transform the Carnival fashion sector by promoting the use of sustainable, locally sourced materials and eliminating hazardous chemicals from costume production. It addresses environmental and health risks posed by materials such as plastic beads, sequins, and metal wire frames that may contain persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and heavy metals. It also fosters gender equity by increasing women’s participation and leadership in the Carnival industry, and disseminates knowledge and practices to other global Carnival events, contributing to broader environmental and socio-economic benefits. The executing partner is the Trinidad-based, Basel Convention Regional Centre for Training and Technology Transfer for the Caribbean (BCRC-Caribbean). To address the debt problem, UN Trade and Development has advocated for a new development-centered international debt architecture. 

This means:

Scaling up concessional finance and grants from multilateral and regional development banks through greater capitalisation and re-channeling of unused Special Drawing Rights to Multilateral Development Banks.
Enhancing international liquidity through improved access to existing Global Financial Safety Net instruments with a focus on fairness and increased quotas for developing countries.
Implementing standstill rules that provide breathing space during crises to boost resilience to external crises. A good example are climate-resilient debt clauses.
Enhancing debt sustainability analysis by reflecting investments in the SDGs.
And making the Common Framework worthwhile for countries in distress

projects.name: Achieving a rapid decarbonization of the energy sector in Saint Kitts and Nevis
projects.description:
The GEF-7 (#10856) Project supports the country in accelerating decarbonization by transitioning towards a highly ambitious target of 100% renewable energy generation. To achieve this, the Government of St. Kitts and Nevis intends to harness renewable energy sources, namely geothermal, solar, wind and waste. It also aims to reduce consumption through achieving 100% high energy e\0fficiency in public buildings. The electrical grid accounts for approximately 65% of the country’s emissions and is therefore the target with the highest potential – especially considering that a decarbonized electricity grid is also a pre-condition for the
future decarbonization of the transport sector. Although Saint Kitts & Nevis' overall emissions are minute (203,036 tCO in 2016), its per capita emissions are relatively large. Electricity generation is responsible for close to 65% of total GHG emissions, as the country relies almost entirely on diesel generators.

A key challenge is to build a comprehensive enabling environment, that can support St. Kitts and Nevis to manage and achieve a transition to decarbonization in a controlled and economically, socially and environmentally viable manner. The GEF incremental logic is that through its \0investment, St. Kitts and Nevis will be able to build upon existing investment to address barriers to decarbonization and achieve its ambitious climate targets. The Project budget is $3,318,995 and is scheduled for completion by 31 December 2027.

projects.name: TTO Trinidad and Tobago E-commerce Strategy Development Project
projects.description:
The need to develop a better understanding of the interface between the digital economy and international trade is increasingly recognized. Over the last couple of decades, e-commerce has emerged as a potentially powerful driver of economic growth, inclusive trade and job-creation in the developing world. However, due to a number of economic, infrastructural, human and financial constraints associated with continuing digital divides across and within them, many developing countries are lagging behind in terms of the readiness to engage in and benefit from e-commerce and the digital economy. The UNCTAD ECDE Programme has developed its policy and technical assistance to support countries requesting assistance in building and maintaining a dynamic and responsive ICT policy environment. It helps to ensure that national ICT programmes become an instrument for supporting relevant components of the national development agenda, enabling local industry to compete in a knowledge-based, global economy, generating better paying jobs, enhancing financial inclusion and standards of living, reducing poverty, and promoting economic growth and export diversification.

Following a request by the Ministry of Trade and Industry, this project aims to develop a national E-commerce Strategy (ECS) for Trinidad and Tobago, to replace the previous strategy (2017-2021) which has come to an end. The project will be delivered under the UNCTAD E-commerce and Digital Economy (ECDE) Programme and will contribute to the efforts by the Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago (GoRTT) to use technology to accelerate change and development, including through economic diversification, job creation and increased trade. Particular focus will be devoted to supporting the use of e-commerce by local businesses to serve domestic, regional and international markets. The project will consist of 3 phases: preparatory phase (with desk review, mapping of stakeholders and dissemination of surveys), diagnostic phase (with the preparation of an eTrade Readiness Assessment that will provide an up-to-date and detailed overview of constraints and opportunities for e-commerce development in key policy areas) and ECS development phase (with the preparation of a national ECS). The project will assist the GoRTT in developing a roadmap for how e-commerce can be used to support trade and technological progress with a view to promoting a more inclusive and sustainable socioeconomic development in the country. By bringing relevant stakeholders together, the project aims to promote a coordinated, whole-of-government output based on participatory process.

The present activity aims to subsequently develop a regional roadmap and guidelines for an effective and relevant integration of the UNESCO ICT competency framework in national frameworks in those countries in order to strengthen teachers’ ICT and competencies and skills. The idea is to offer countries a more comprehensive set of competencies and skills that teachers need to integrate ICT into their professional pedagogies and practices in order to facilitate students’ achievement of curricular objectives. It is envisaged that once developed, the roadmap will be submitted to a consultation across different stakeholders and will be validated through a regional workshop bringing together ministries of education representatives of the different countries.

projects.name: TTO Technical support in establishing a National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI) in Trinidad and Tobago.
projects.description: A robust National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI) is a necessary component for enhancing capabilities in spatial data management, improving, and strengthening decision-making and response mechanisms that support sustainable development. It fosters data accessibility, interoperability, reliability, and currency across all sectors of society. A comprehensive situational analysis is essential to understanding the current state, existing challenges, and opportunities within a nation's spatial data landscape, which paves the way for the development of a robust NSDI. The Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago, through the Ministry of Land and Legal Affairs (MLLA), requested technical support from the Economic Commission of Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) to establish an NSDI that aligns with global standards and best practices. This technical service included a comprehensive situational and gap analysis for the MLLA and its agencies and provide a roadmap (including timelines) for advancing on the achievement of an NSDI with the MLLA as the lead national body.

projects.description: The ACP MEAs-III Project is being implemented by UNEP (Components 1 & 3) and FAO (Component 3). The Project is a partnership between the European Commission, the Secretariat of the African, Caribbean and Pacific group of states (ACP), the United Nations Environment Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations. The aim is to empower key stakeholders to address environmental challenges and improve environmental management at the national and regional levels.  The first two Project phases focused on capacity capacity building activities for regional inter-governmental organisations, governments and stakeholders, who have been equipped with the appropriate knowledge and tools to i) participate in international negotiations (i.e. Conventions of Parties); ii) mainstream MEAs commitments into national policies; iii) develop environmental legislation and management tools that serve the implementation of MEAs commitments; and iv) ensure monitoring and reporting of the implementation of MEAs and on the impact of these efforts on the environment in their respective territories.  The objective of this third phase of the ACP MEAs programme is to enhance the mainstreaming and implementation of biodiversity and chemicals and waste MEAs with a focus on: i) the mainstreaming of biodiversity in agriculture, ii) the management of chemicals and waste (including hazardous pesticides), iii) the reinforcement of compliance and enforcement measures and iv) the strengthening of the implementation of regional seas conventions in ACP countries.  There were no national allocations for Caribbean countries.

projects.description: The Sint Maarten Dutch Quarter Water and Sanitation project supports the rehabilitation and expansion of critical wastewater and urban infrastructure in a densely populated community. The project focuses on upgrading and completing sewerage infrastructure, including wastewater collection and conveyance systems, pumping infrastructure and connections required to improve sanitation services and reduce environmental and public health risks. Planned works include completion of the pumping station, rationalization of existing intermediate infrastructure, connection of sewerage pressure lines and the progressive establishment of residential house connections. The intervention also incorporates complementary public infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlighting, to improve accessibility and safety within the project area. Together, these investments aim to provide more reliable and resilient sanitation infrastructure, improve living conditions in Dutch Quarter and support safer, healthier and more sustainable urban development for residents and businesses.

Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
children.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.
